bodyLanguage.title: Grounded Stance
bodyLanguage.goal: Stand so you look and feel immovable: weight centred, no swaying, shuffling or hip-popping.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Face a mirror. Feet about hip-width, toes slightly out, knees soft (not locked). Rock gently forward/back and side to side, then settle where weight is spread evenly over both feet.
1:00-2:30 - Arms relaxed at your sides. Hold completely still for 90 seconds. Each time you catch a weight shift or sway, reset and note it. Target: zero shifts in the last 30 seconds.

2:30-4:00 - Keep the stance and say aloud 3 times, slowly: 'Good morning. I'm the clinical pharmacist on this team. I've reviewed all the medication profiles.' Feet and hips must not move while you talk.
4:00-5:00 - Record 30 seconds of the same lines on your phone. Watch on mute and count every sway, foot shuffle or hip pop. Write the number down: this is your baseline.
bodyLanguage.why: Swaying, weight-shifting and foot-shuffling are movement with no message, so observers tend to read them as restlessness or discomfort. There is no controlled trial of a 'grounded stance'; this is a coaching fundamental. It matters because every later exercise (gestures, voice, gaze) looks more deliberate when the lower body is quiet.
bodyLanguage.specter: The person who doesn't need to move is the one the whole room ends up watching.

bodyLanguage.title: Tall Spine, Level Chin
bodyLanguage.goal: Make upright posture with a level chin your default, and learn to reset to it in one breath, without believing the power-pose hormone myths.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Stand side-on to a mirror. Imagine a string lifting the crown of your head. Roll shoulders up, back, and let them drop. Ears roughly over shoulders, chin parallel to the floor.
1:00-2:00 - Chin calibration: tilt chin up ~2 cm (reads as looking down on people), down ~2 cm (reads as hiding), then level. Repeat 5 times until level feels normal.
2:00-4:00 - Hold the posture and read aloud 4 times: 'Today's priority patients are bed 4, bed 9 and bed 12. I'll start with bed 4.' Check ear-over-shoulder alignment after each.
4:00-5:00 - Slump fully for 10 seconds, then reset to tall in a single breath. 4 cycles. The skill is the fast reset, not holding stiffly all day.
5:00-6:00 - Choose 3 posture cues for today (e.g. badging in, opening a patient chart, entering the lift) and reset each time.
bodyLanguage.why: Be honest about the evidence. The 2010 power-pose claims (higher testosterone, lower cortisol, more risk-taking) failed replication: Ranehill et al. (2015, N=200) found an effect on self-reported feelings of power but none on hormones or behaviour, and the original first author, Dana Carney, said in 2016 that she no longer believes power-pose effects are real. The p-curve debate that followed (Simmons & Simonsohn, 2017; Cuddy, Schultz & Fosse, 2018) narrowed the defensible claim to 'felt power', and Crede (2019) pointed out that most of those studies had no neutral-posture group; in the few that did, the difference came almost entirely from the slumped pose making people feel worse, not from the expansive pose making them feel better. A 2022 meta-analysis (Korner et al., Psychological Bulletin; 88 studies, 9,779 people) found modest effects of posture on self-reported feelings, behavioural effects that looked inflated by publication bias and outliers, and no effect on hormones or other physiology. Effects were also larger when participants could more easily guess the study's aim, so expectation may explain part of them. So train posture to avoid the slump and for how you come across, not for hormones or a guaranteed confidence boost.
bodyLanguage.specter: Stand like you've already read the file, because you have.

bodyLanguage.title: Stillness Baseline: Count Your Fidgets
bodyLanguage.goal: Find your personal fidget habits on video and cut them by half.
steps: 0:00-1:30 - Record yourself (standing, waist up, hands visible) explaining a recent clinical intervention for 60 seconds, as you would to a colleague. Don't try to be still yet.

1:30-3:00 - Watch it on mute. Tally every non-purposeful movement: touching face, hair or beard, adjusting glasses or headwear, clicking a pen, rubbing hands, rocking, shrugging. Write down the total and your top 2 habits.
3:00-4:00 - Record the same 60-second story again. Rule: hands either gesture with meaning or rest. When you feel the urge for a top habit, hold still and finish the sentence first.
4:00-6:00 - Watch take 2 on mute, tally again and compare. Target: at least 50% fewer in take 2. Keep both numbers for Day 28.
bodyLanguage.why: In a preregistered study (Chertoff & Mesler, University of Lethbridge, 2026; N=388), people who watched a short video of someone fidgeting during a game of checkers rated that person higher in emotionality, which includes anxiety, and lower in agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness than viewers of a version where both players sat still. It is a single study of a person who wasn't speaking, so treat it as a strong hint rather than settled fact. Video counting works because most fidgets are automatic and invisible to you in the moment.
bodyLanguage.specter: Every unnecessary movement is a leak. Plug the leaks and what's left is signal.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Adjusting headwear (shemagh, ghutra, hijab or niqab) is a very common habit. One deliberate adjustment before you start speaking is fine; repeated touching mid-sentence reads as nervousness.

bodyLanguage.title: Head Stillness and the Slow Nod
bodyLanguage.goal: Keep your head still while you speak, and swap rapid repeated nodding for one slow, deliberate nod.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Mirror. Say 'The dose is appropriate for her renal function.' Watch for head bobbing or tilting on each word. Repeat until the head stays still for the whole sentence.
1:00-2:30 - Contrast drill: 5 quick nods (the anxious 'yes-yes-yes'), then 1 slow nod: down over about 1 second, brief pause, up over about 1 second. Do the pair 5 times so you feel the difference.
2:30-4:00 - Play 90 seconds of any lecture or podcast. Listen as if in a meeting and give a single slow nod only when you genuinely agree with a point: 3-4 nods maximum.
4:00-5:00 - 'Acknowledge, then answer' aloud 3 times: slow nod, 1-second pause, then 'Understood. Here's what I recommend.'
bodyLanguage.why: Rapid, repeated nodding reads as eagerness to please; one slower nod signals that you've weighed the point and accept it. Extra head movement while you speak also competes with your words. This is coaching practice, not a tested intervention.
bodyLanguage.specter: Agree slowly. It makes your agreement worth something.
bodyLanguage.cultural: In Saudi conversation, nods and short acknowledgments ('na'am', 'tamam') are polite and expected, especially with seniors. Keep them; just make them single and unhurried rather than continuous.

bodyLanguage.title: The Composed Resting Face
bodyLanguage.goal: Build a relaxed, composed resting face (loose jaw, smooth brow, soft eyes) and switch deliberately between warm and neutral.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Mirror. Tense your whole face for 5 seconds, then release. 3 times. Notice what jaw, brow and lips feel like at rest.
1:00-2:30 - Jaw: teeth slightly apart behind closed lips, tongue resting. Brow: smooth the space between your eyebrows. Hold this neutral face for 60 seconds while breathing normally.

2:30-4:00 - Every 10 seconds, switch between neutral and a genuine small smile (eyes slightly narrowed, not just the mouth). Say 'Good morning, how are you today?' with the warm face and 'That combination isn't safe' with the neutral face.
4:00-5:00 - Selfie video: hold the neutral face for 20 seconds while thinking about a stressful case. Look for tight lips, raised brows or a frown. Repeat until the neutral face holds.
bodyLanguage.why: A tight jaw, a furrowed brow and pressed lips are easily read as stress, irritation or disapproval, even when you're only concentrating. The goal is not to hide emotion but to choose which expression you show: warm for rapport, neutral for a firm clinical point. Coaching practice; no trial of this specific drill.
bodyLanguage.specter: Your face shouldn't tell them the score before you do.

bodyLanguage.title: Home Base for Nervous Hands
bodyLanguage.goal: Have three default hand positions so your hands never wander, fidget or hide.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Learn the 3 home bases: (1) arms relaxed at your sides; (2) hands loosely together at navel height, one resting in the other; (3) seated, forearms on the table with hands visible and still.
1:00-2:30 - Mirror: hold each home base for 30 seconds. Check for fists, white knuckles, hand-wringing or rubbing thumbs, and loosen them.

2:30-4:00 - Say these lines, making one gesture per sentence and returning to a home base after each: 'There are two problems with this regimen.' / 'First, the dose is too high.' / 'Second, there's an interaction with amiodarone.'
4:00-5:00 - Ban-list check: hands in pockets, arms tightly crossed, hands hidden behind your back while talking, clicking a pen. Rule for today: put the pen down before you speak.
bodyLanguage.why: Hidden or busy hands draw attention and are commonly read as discomfort, and in one study watching someone fidget lowered observers' trait ratings (see b03). Deciding in advance where your hands rest removes the 'what do I do with my hands?' problem that drives fidgeting. The positions themselves are coaching conventions.
bodyLanguage.specter: Hands at rest say you're not reaching for anything.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Indicate people with an open hand rather than a pointed finger, and use your right hand to pass documents or medications; both are customary courtesy in Saudi Arabia.

bodyLanguage.title: The Deliberate Pause Before Answering
bodyLanguage.goal: Replace instant or filler-led answers with a calm 1-2 second pause, so your answer sounds considered and certain.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - List 6 questions you get often, e.g. 'Is this dose OK?', 'Can we give this through a feeding tube?', 'Why not the brand?', 'Do we really need to hold it?'

1:00-4:00 - For each: read it aloud (or play a recording of yourself asking it), then pause: lips closed, one quiet breath through the nose, neutral face, eyes up or briefly down to think, count 'one-two' silently. Then answer with the conclusion first, e.g. 'Yes. Give 40 mg once daily.'
4:00-5:00 - Redo 3 questions with nothing in front of the answer: no 'um', 'so', 'actually' or 'basically'.
5:00-6:00 - Record one answer and check that the pause looks like thinking, not freezing: still body, relaxed face, then a clean answer.
bodyLanguage.why: A short silent pause does two jobs. It replaces the filler: listeners treat 'um' and a rising tone as signs that a speaker is unsure (Brennan & Williams, 1995), and in real, unscripted speech filled pauses lowered ratings of a speaker's readiness and certainty (Lee & Papafragou; more on Day 18). It also buys retrieval time: Glenberg et al. (1998) found people avert their gaze more as questions get harder, and that doing so helps them remember, so a brief look away while you think is normal, not evasive. Keep the pause short, because long hesitations can also read as doubt; the 1-2 second figure is a coaching rule, not a measured optimum.
bodyLanguage.specter: Answer when you're ready, not when they're impatient.
bodyLanguage.cultural: With a senior consultant or an elder, a brief pause and a slight nod before answering is polite and shows you're taking the question seriously.

bodyLanguage.title: The Unhurried Walk
bodyLanguage.goal: Walk at a deliberate pace with full strides and a quiet upper body through corridors, wards and into meetings.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Walk 10 steps at your usual pace, then 10 steps at about 80% of that speed with a full stride (no shuffling). Notice the difference.
1:00-3:00 - Walk a loop for 2 minutes: head level, eyes at horizon height (not on the floor or a phone), arms swinging naturally, shoulders down, nothing in your hands.

3:00-4:30 - Stop-and-turn drill: walk, stop on a mark, stand fully still for 2 seconds, turn your whole body (not just your head) toward an imagined colleague and say 'Doctor, do you have a minute about bed 7?' 5 repetitions.
4:30-6:00 - Record 20 seconds of walking toward the camera. Check for bouncing, hurrying, looking down, or arms clamped to your sides.
bodyLanguage.why: Rushing usually reads as stress or being behind; a steady pace with a level head reads as composed. No controlled study is relied on here; this is a practitioner principle. In a real emergency, move fast: the goal is urgency without panic.
bodyLanguage.specter: Walk like you know where you're going and what you'll say when you get there.

bodyLanguage.title: Entering the Room: The Two-Second Pause
bodyLanguage.goal: Enter a ward, office or meeting with a brief pause and a scan, then move with purpose.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Use a real door at home: open it fully, step in one pace, stop.
1:00-2:30 - The pause: stand still for 2 seconds, scan left to right at face height, pick your destination, then walk there. 5 entries.
2:30-4:00 - Add the greeting: after the scan, look at the most senior person (or the person you came to see) and say 'Assalamu alaikum. Good morning, everyone.' Then walk to your place. 4 entries.
4:00-5:00 - Practise the exit: finish your sentence, slow nod, 'Thank you,' turn and leave without rushing or backing out.
5:00-6:00 - Plan today's two real entrances (e.g. morning round, a meeting) and do them this way.
bodyLanguage.why: First seconds shape impressions, and a brief pause shows you're neither rushed nor asking permission to be there. This is coaching practice without a specific trial behind it. Keep the pause short (about 2 seconds) so it reads as composure, not hesitation.
bodyLanguage.specter: One beat at the door, see the room, then walk in like you have a reason to be there, because you do.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Saudi etiquette is to greet the eldest or most senior person present first, and the scan helps you find them. A group 'Assalamu alaikum' is natural and appreciated. If that person is of the opposite gender, greet them by title with a brief look and a lowered gaze rather than holding eye contact. A patient's room is different: knock, say 'Assalamu alaikum, may I come in?' and wait for permission (or for the nurse or the patient's companion to prepare the patient), especially on women's wards and as your hospital's chaperone policy requires. Take your pause at the doorway or curtain, not inside.

bodyLanguage.title: Sitting Like You Belong
bodyLanguage.goal: Sit fully back, upright and settled, forearms on the table: never perched on the edge, never sprawled.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Sit at a table: hips all the way back in the chair, spine upright (lightly touching the backrest is fine), feet flat.
1:00-2:00 - Forearms on the table, hands visible, shoulders down. Hold 60 seconds without touching your face or phone.

2:00-3:30 - Lean-in drill: on a key point, lean forward about 10 degrees from the hips and say 'This is the part that matters. The interaction is clinically significant.' Then return to upright. 4 times.
3:30-4:30 - Contrast: perch on the edge with hands in your lap (reads nervous), then lean far back with hands behind your head (reads arrogant). Return to the middle.
4:30-5:00 - Before your next meeting starts: notes laid out, phone face-down, settled in your seat.
bodyLanguage.why: People who were trying to look intelligent tended to sit up straighter (Murphy, 2007), but reports of that study disagree on whether posture itself raised observers' ratings; looking at your partner while speaking was the clearer cue. A forward lean on key points directs attention. The middle position avoids both submissive perching and dominant sprawling; these details are coaching practice.
bodyLanguage.specter: Sit like your seat at the table was never in question.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Avoid pointing the soles of your feet or shoes at anyone (e.g. ankle on knee). In a majlis or a meeting with seniors, wait for the eldest or most senior person to sit first, let the host guide seating, and sit upright.

bodyLanguage.title: Slow, Deliberate Gestures
bodyLanguage.goal: Cut aimless movement and make each gesture slower, complete and inside the 'gesture box', so every movement adds meaning.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - The gesture box: shoulders to waist, about shoulder-width. In front of a mirror, trace its edges with both hands.

1:00-3:00 - Say: 'We have three options. Option one, reduce the dose. Option two, switch agents. Option three, monitor and wait.' One clear gesture per option (place each option in the air left, centre, right), at half your usual speed, holding each gesture for a moment.
3:00-4:30 - Record it once with fast, chopping gestures and once at half speed. Watch both on mute and decide which looks in control.
4:30-6:00 - Repeat 3 times at half speed, finishing every gesture back at a home base (b06).
bodyLanguage.why: Fast, jerky or aimless movement is easily read as nervous energy, while slower, completed gestures look controlled. Direct research on gesture speed is limited, so this part is coaching practice. The aim is not fewer gestures overall: the best evidence (Day 13) favours gestures that picture what you're saying, so cut the aimless ones and keep the meaningful ones. The gesture box keeps hands visible and in the listener's line of sight without becoming theatrical.
bodyLanguage.specter: No wasted motion: if your hands move, they're saying something.

bodyLanguage.title: Open Palms vs Palm-Down
bodyLanguage.goal: Use open palms to signal openness and palm-down gestures to signal firmness, on purpose.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Mirror. Palms up, slightly open, at waist height: 'Let me explain my reasoning.' Palm down, flat, moving slightly downward: 'That dose isn't safe.'

1:00-3:00 - Six lines, palm direction matched to the message: 'I'm open to your thoughts' (up) / 'Here are the options' (up, offering) / 'This is the maximum dose' (down) / 'We need to stop the infusion now' (down) / 'What would work for you?' (up) / 'I can't support that dose' (down).
3:00-4:00 - Remove: pointing at people, chopping toward someone, hands in pockets.
4:00-5:00 - Record 3 of the lines and check that palm direction matches each message.
bodyLanguage.why: Visible open hands are widely taught as a cue of openness, and palm-down movements as a cue of firmness. These meanings come from coaching convention rather than strong controlled studies, so use them as consistent signals, not proven persuasion levers.
bodyLanguage.specter: Show your hands when you're open; flatten them when the matter's closed.
bodyLanguage.cultural: A downward-pushing hand aimed at a senior or an elder can look like you're instructing them; with seniors, keep the firmness in your words and use a level, still hand. To call someone over, use the whole hand rather than a curled finger.

bodyLanguage.title: Illustrator Gestures
bodyLanguage.goal: Use gestures that picture what you're saying (size, trend, sequence, comparison): the gesture type with the best experimental evidence.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Learn 4 illustrators: SIZE (hands apart for big or increase, close for small); TREND (hand rising for increasing, falling for decreasing); SEQUENCE (place steps left to right); COMPARISON (one hand for 'this', the other for 'that').

1:00-4:00 - Say each line with the matching illustrator, 3 times each: 'Her creatinine has doubled since Monday' (rising hand) / 'The dose needs to come down by half' (hand lowering) / 'First we load, then we maintain' (left, then right) / 'Option A is cheaper; option B is safer' (left hand, right hand).
4:00-5:30 - Give a 60-second explanation of a drug interaction to the camera using at least 3 illustrators.
5:30-7:00 - Watch on mute. Could someone guess part of the message from your hands alone? Redo the parts where the gestures were random.
bodyLanguage.why: Cascio Rizzo, Berger and Zhou (Journal of Marketing Research, 2025) analysed 2,184 TED talks and ran preregistered experiments with about 1,600 participants. Speakers using illustrator gestures, which depict what is being said, were rated clearer, more competent and more persuasive than when they used 'highlighter' gestures that only add emphasis, or unrelated movement, mainly because illustrators make the message easier to process. This fits an earlier meta-analysis of 63 samples (Hostetter, 2011, Psychological Bulletin) that found gestures give listeners a moderate comprehension boost, largest when the gesture adds information to the words. Caveat: the persuasion experiments used short consumer-product pitches, so the size of the effect in clinical talk is unknown.
bodyLanguage.specter: Don't just say the number. Show them how big it is.

bodyLanguage.title: Steepling: When and When Not
bodyLanguage.goal: Use the steeple (fingertips touching) as an occasional calm 'listening in control' position without overusing it.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Seated, forearms on the table. Bring fingertips together with palms apart, at lower-chest height: not at your face, not raised high.
1:00-2:30 - Play a 60-second audio clip. While listening, hold the steeple for 15-20 seconds, release smoothly to a home base, repeat.
2:30-4:00 - Speaking drill: open the steeple into an open-palm gesture as you start: 'I've thought about this. My recommendation is to switch to oral today.' Then return to a home base. 4 times.
4:00-5:00 - Rule for today: no more than 2-3 steeples per meeting, only while listening or pausing, and never while a senior is criticising you.
bodyLanguage.why: The steeple is popular in body-language books as a confidence cue, but no strong controlled research shows it raises perceived authority, and overuse looks staged or smug. Its real value is as a calm, still place for your hands while you listen.
bodyLanguage.specter: Real confidence is quiet: one steeple, not ten.
bodyLanguage.cultural: With very senior figures in conservative settings, a steeple can look overly self-assured; hands resting quietly on the table is safer.

bodyLanguage.title: Land the Sentence: Downward Endings
bodyLanguage.goal: End statements with a falling pitch so recommendations sound like conclusions, not questions.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Say 'We should hold the metformin' twice: once rising at the end like a question, once falling. Feel the difference.

1:00-3:00 - Read 6 recommendations, letting your pitch drop slightly on the last word and stopping cleanly: 'I recommend stopping the clopidogrel.' / 'The level is therapeutic.' / 'We switch to oral today.' / 'This needs a renal dose adjustment.' / 'Start potassium replacement now.' / 'No further changes.'
3:00-4:30 - Record 3 of the lines. Does each sound like an answer? Redo any that rise.
4:30-6:00 - Lower, not forced: speak from a relaxed chest voice and don't push your voice down. If it strains, stop and speak normally.
bodyLanguage.why: In laboratory studies with digitally altered recordings, listeners preferred lower-pitched voices for leadership, for both men's and women's voices (Klofstad, Anderson & Peters, 2012), and a follow-up linked that preference to lower voices sounding stronger and more competent (Klofstad, Anderson & Nowicki, 2015); men's voices lowered in pitch were also rated more dominant (Puts, Gaulin & Verdolini, 2006). These studies used altered recordings in hypothetical settings and do not show that forcing your own voice lower helps, so this drill deliberately does not train pitch level. What it trains is intonation: listeners use tone of voice as a cue to how sure a speaker is, and a rising end makes a statement sound like a question (Brennan & Williams, 1995). That rests on a small number of lab studies, so treat it as a sensible habit rather than a proven persuasion effect.
bodyLanguage.specter: A recommendation ends with a full stop, not a question mark.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Clinical discussion in Saudi hospitals is often in English and social talk in Arabic; practise falling endings in both languages.

bodyLanguage.title: Slow the Tempo
bodyLanguage.goal: Find your real speaking rate and, if you rush, slow to a deliberate pace with short pauses between ideas.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Record yourself reading a ~100-word paragraph (e.g. part of a drug monograph) at your usual speed. Words divided by seconds, times 60, gives your words per minute.

1:00-3:00 - If you were fast (as a rough coaching guide, much above about 170 words per minute is hard to follow on dense clinical content), record it again about 15-20% slower. If you were already below that, keep your speed. Either way, add a short pause at every full stop and a longer one between key points. Keep the energy up: deliberate, not sleepy.
3:00-4:30 - Explain a case for 60 seconds at your new pace, using pauses instead of 'and so... and then...'.
4:30-6:00 - Play both paragraph recordings and mark which sounds more in command and easier to follow.
bodyLanguage.why: Fast, run-on speech often sounds nervous and makes complex clinical information harder to follow; slowing slightly and pausing between ideas improves clarity. No single speaking rate has been shown to maximise authority. A University of Michigan analysis of 1,380 survey-introduction calls (Benki et al., presented at a 2011 conference, not peer-reviewed) found interviewers who spoke moderately fast, about 3.5 words per second, did better than very fast or very slow ones, and those who never paused did worst. So slow down only if you rush: aim for deliberate with pauses, not slow motion.
bodyLanguage.specter: Rushing is for people afraid of being interrupted.

bodyLanguage.title: Volume That Reaches the Team
bodyLanguage.goal: Be clearly heard by everyone on the round or in the meeting, without shouting and all the way to the last word, while keeping patient details private.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Stand 3-4 metres from a wall (about the far side of a ward-round group). Breathe low into your belly.

1:00-3:00 - Say 'Good morning. I have three medication updates.' toward the wall at 3 levels: conversational, projected (the far side of the group hears you easily), and one notch louder (once only, without straining). Settle on projected.
3:00-4:00 - Keep the volume through the final word: 'The INR is three point eight.' The last word should be as loud as the first. 5 times.

4:00-5:00 - Record from across the room: can you hear every word? Then say one line at shared-bay volume: clear to someone 1-2 metres away, not to the next bed. If your throat feels tight or scratchy at any point, drop the volume and stop for today.
bodyLanguage.why: Trailing off at sentence ends or speaking too quietly on a noisy ward means people miss your recommendation, and you can sound unsure. Projecting from the breath rather than the throat is standard voice-care advice. Volume should match the audience, not the room: on a shared bay or with visitors nearby, patient details belong at team volume. Coaching practice, not a researched intervention.
bodyLanguage.specter: Say it once, clearly enough that nobody has to ask again.
bodyLanguage.cultural: In Saudi social settings a raised voice can read as anger; project for clarity, not force, especially with elders. A family companion often stays at the bedside, so keep sensitive details at team volume or step aside to discuss them.

bodyLanguage.title: Kill the Fillers
bodyLanguage.goal: Replace 'um', 'uh', 'like' and 'basically' with silence, especially in front of a recommendation.
steps: 0:00-2:00 - Record a 60-second explanation (e.g. why an antibiotic needs adjusting). Play it back and count the fillers.
2:00-4:00 - Record it again. Whenever you feel a filler coming, close your lips and pause silently instead.
4:00-5:00 - Pause-first drill: '[pause] The culture came back. [pause] It's sensitive to cefazolin. [pause] We can de-escalate today.' 3 times.
5:00-6:00 - Play back the second recording and count again. Target: half the first count. Keep both numbers for Day 28.
bodyLanguage.why: In a study using real, unscripted speech (Lee & Papafragou, Cognitive Science Society proceedings), filled pauses lowered listeners' ratings of a speaker's readiness and certainty for experts and novices alike, and listeners were less willing to go back to a disfluent speaker, although disfluent experts were also seen as more careful. Brennan and Williams (1995) likewise showed listeners treat fillers as a sign of uncertainty. Some fillers are normal in natural speech; the aim is not zero fillers but no filler in front of a recommendation.
bodyLanguage.specter: Silence buys you time; 'um' spends your credibility.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Arabic fillers such as 'ya'ni' or 'ba'dain' count too when they come in front of a clinical point.

bodyLanguage.title: Hold Your Place in the Group
bodyLanguage.goal: On rounds and in meetings, stand where you can be seen and heard, at a respectful distance, without shrinking to the back or crowding anyone.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Picture your usual ward round: where do you stand? Many pharmacists drift to the back or the edge. Choose a target spot in the front arc of the group, with a clear line of sight to the lead clinician and the chart or screen.

1:00-2:00 - Distance check against a wall or doorframe: about one arm's length from a same-gender colleague, a step more across genders. Stand there with feet hip-width, weight centred and hands at a home base (b06).

2:00-3:30 - Contrast drill: shrink (half behind an imagined colleague, notes clutched to your chest) for 10 seconds, crowd (step into the centre, elbow out, leaning toward the speaker) for 10 seconds, then settle in your target spot. 3 rounds.
3:30-5:00 - From your spot, take a half-step into the circle and say 'Before we move on, one medication point on bed 8,' then step back once you've finished. 3 times.
bodyLanguage.why: A meta-analysis of nonverbal behaviour and status (Hall, Coats & LeBeau, 2005) found that people believe cues such as open, expansive posture and position signal dominance and high status, but that these beliefs are stronger and more widespread than the actual links. So where and how you stand changes how you are read more than what you are, and a recommendation from the back of the group is easy to miss. The specific spot and distances are coaching judgment, not findings of that meta-analysis.
bodyLanguage.specter: Own your space; don't annex anyone else's.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Keep more distance across genders; same-gender colleagues may stand closer than in Western settings. Don't compete with a senior for the spot beside the consultant; take a visible place in the arc instead.

bodyLanguage.title: Stand When You Present
bodyLanguage.goal: Default to standing when you present a case, data or a recommendation to a group.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Prepare a 60-second case summary: patient, problem, recommendation.
1:00-3:00 - Deliver it seated, then standing (grounded feet, home-base hands). Record both.
3:00-5:00 - Standing version again, adding a 2-second pause before you start, falling endings, and one illustrator gesture per key point.
5:00-7:00 - Finish with 'Any questions?', hold still for 3 seconds, then 'Thank you.' Check the playback for leaning on the table or swaying.
bodyLanguage.why: Standing makes you more visible, frees your breath and arms, and marks the moment as a presentation. This is coaching practice without a specific trial. Read the room: in a small seated discussion, standing alone can feel too formal.
bodyLanguage.specter: When it's your case, take the floor.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Standing to greet a senior or an elder who joins the meeting is a common courtesy in Saudi workplaces. When presenting to leadership, follow the meeting's norm: if everyone presents seated, sit upright and present from your seat.

bodyLanguage.title: Handshake, and Greetings Without One
bodyLanguage.goal: Greet with confidence: a right-handed handshake matched to the other person's grip and pace where appropriate, and a respectful no-touch greeting where not.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Handshake form (with a same-gender family member or a rolled towel): right hand, web of thumb to web of thumb, a medium grip you can adjust (never crushing). Practise two versions: a brief 2-second shake (common with many Western colleagues) and a lighter, longer one held through the greeting (common between Saudis of the same gender).

1:00-2:30 - Add eyes and words: look, smile, 'Assalamu alaikum. I'm [name], the clinical pharmacist.' In the longer version, keep hold through 'Kaif halak?' (to a woman, 'Kaif halik?') and the reply, and let the other person decide when to release. 5 times.
2:30-4:00 - No-touch greeting: right hand on the heart, slight nod, a brief warm glance (or lowered gaze), 'Assalamu alaikum, nice to meet you.' 5 times.

4:00-5:00 - Decision rule: with someone of the opposite gender, greet verbally with a nod or hand on heart and never reach first. If you yourself don't shake hands across genders and a hand is offered, keep your right hand on your chest, smile and say 'Pleased to meet you' warmly; rehearse this once aloud.
5:00-6:00 - Rehearse aloud: meeting a new consultant (same gender); meeting a new head nurse (opposite gender).
bodyLanguage.why: In an fMRI study, 18 volunteers watched animated videos of business interactions; those that began with a handshake were rated more favourably, and the handshake softened the impact of avoidant behaviour (Dolcos et al., 2012). The 'firm handshake' advice comes from US studies such as Chaplin et al. (2000; 112 students), where a firmer grip went with more favourable first impressions. Both are small and culturally specific, so the evidence is weak. Between Saudis of the same gender, matching the other person's grip and pace matters more than firmness (a coaching judgment).
bodyLanguage.specter: Let them set the length of the greeting; you set the agenda after it.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Between men, or between women, the common Saudi greeting is a handshake with 'Assalamu alaikum' (reply 'Wa alaikum assalam'). It is often lighter and longer than a Western handshake, and close friends or relatives may add cheek kisses. Greet the eldest or most senior person first. Many Saudi Muslims, men and women, do not shake hands with the opposite gender for religious reasons: greet verbally with a nod or a hand on the heart, never initiate a cross-gender handshake, and don't extend your hand to a woman wearing niqab. If you don't shake hands across genders and one is offered, a hand on the heart with a smile and a warm greeting is widely understood and polite, not rude.

bodyLanguage.title: Careful Mirroring
bodyLanguage.goal: Build rapport by matching pace, volume and energy, not by copying gestures.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Watch a 60-second interview clip. Note the person's speaking speed, volume, energy and posture.
1:00-3:00 - Pause the clip and answer aloud as if to them, matching their tempo and energy (calm and slow, or brisk and crisp).
3:00-4:30 - Posture echo: when they lean forward, wait 5-10 seconds, then take up a similar (not identical) posture. Never copy within a second, never move for move.

4:30-6:00 - Lead test: after matching, gradually slow and calm your own voice. In real life, notice whether the other person follows. With an angry family member, match their seriousness, not their anger.
bodyLanguage.why: Chartrand and Bargh (1999) found that being subtly mimicked made interactions feel smoother and increased liking, and a 2016 meta-analysis (Vicaria & Dickens) linked mimicry and coordination to better rapport. But results are not consistent: in the preregistered second study of Hale and Hamilton (2016), mimicry by a virtual partner had no effect on rapport or trust. The original effects came from mimicry people didn't consciously notice; obvious copying is untested and likely to look odd. Matching tempo and energy, which this drill trains, has been studied less than copying gestures, so treat it as a sensible rapport habit, not a reliable lever.
bodyLanguage.specter: Meet them at their pace, then set the pace.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Mirroring includes formality: if a senior uses formal greetings and titles ('Dr.', 'Ustadh'), match that before moving to anything casual.

bodyLanguage.title: Use Silence After Your Point
bodyLanguage.goal: After a key statement, offer or refusal, stop talking and hold the silence.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Write 4 end lines: a recommendation, a price, a refusal, a question.

1:00-3:00 - For each: say it once, then stay silent and still for 3-5 seconds (count silently) with a relaxed face, and use the time to think about what the other side needs. No extra explanation, no softeners, no 'does that make sense?'.
3:00-4:30 - Negotiation run: 'Our ceiling is 1.2 million riyals.' 3-5 seconds of silence. 'If you include on-site training, we can sign this quarter.' 3-5 seconds of silence. 3 times.
4:30-6:00 - Record and watch: during the silence, are you nodding, smiling nervously or touching your face? Remove it and redo.
bodyLanguage.why: The best evidence on silence in negotiation (Curhan et al., 2022, Journal of Applied Psychology; four studies) found that pauses of 3 seconds or more, whether natural or instructed, led to deals that created more value for both sides, because they put negotiators into a more deliberative, less 'fixed-pie' frame of mind. The authors found no sign that silence worked by intimidating the other side, and it helped when the higher-status party used it but not the lower-status one. So treat silence as thinking time that lets your point land, not as a pressure weapon, and keep it short with seniors. Not over-explaining after you state a position is standard negotiation-training advice. One paper, mostly about value creation, so the evidence is weak for other situations.
bodyLanguage.specter: Say it once. The silence after is where they decide.
bodyLanguage.cultural: In Saudi business, relationships usually come before terms: use silence after a position, not as a cold opener, and keep a warm face so it reads as patience. With a senior consultant or manager, a 2-3 second pause is respectful; a long stand-off silence can feel like defiance.

bodyLanguage.title: Composure Under Pushback
bodyLanguage.goal: Keep face, body and voice steady when challenged, then respond with substance.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Write 4 typical challenges: 'Why are you questioning my order?' / 'We've always done it this way.' / 'That's not your call.' / 'Just approve it.'

1:00-4:00 - Have someone read them, or record and play them back. For each: neutral face, still body, home-base hands, 2-second pause, then calmly: 'I understand. My concern is patient safety: the dose exceeds the renal maximum. Here's an alternative.'
4:00-5:30 - Check the video for leaks: eye-roll, pressed lips, smirk, sharp breath in, arms crossing.
5:30-7:00 - Repeat the two hardest challenges until your face stays neutral the whole time.
bodyLanguage.why: Defensive expressions and sudden movements escalate conflict and show you've been rattled; a neutral face and a structured answer keep the focus on the clinical issue. 'Acknowledge, state the concern, offer an alternative' is a common de-escalation pattern, not a tested intervention.
bodyLanguage.specter: When they push, get calmer, not louder.
bodyLanguage.cultural: Many Saudi workplaces value face-saving, especially toward seniors. For a concern that can wait, raise it privately and respectfully ('Doctor, may I share a concern?') rather than contradicting a senior in front of the team. If harm is imminent, for example the dose is about to be given, speak up at once, calmly and specifically, whoever is present: patient safety comes before face.

bodyLanguage.title: Listening Presence
bodyLanguage.goal: Look fully engaged while listening: still body, steady gaze, few but clear acknowledgments.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Play a 2-3 minute talk. Sit upright, phone out of reach.
1:00-4:00 - Listen with a still head, eyes on the speaker's face, the occasional slow nod and no fidgeting. Pause twice to summarise aloud: 'So the main concern is...'
4:00-5:00 - Lean in slightly when the key point arrives.
5:00-6:00 - Plan for today: in your next real conversation, wait one full second after the person finishes before you reply.
bodyLanguage.why: Looking at your partner was linked to higher perceived intelligence in Murphy (2007), most clearly while speaking. Good listening also changes the speaker: in four lab experiments, people who were listened to attentively and without judgment reported less social anxiety, became more aware of both sides of their own views and held them less extremely (Itzchakov, Kluger & Castro, 2017). Watching someone fidget lowered observers' trait ratings (Chertoff & Mesler; see b03). Summarising shows you processed what was said and gives you your next move. The one-second wait is a coaching rule.
bodyLanguage.specter: Hear the whole thing. The detail you need is usually in the last sentence.
bodyLanguage.cultural: When listening to an elder or a senior consultant, a slightly softer, lower gaze with nods and 'na'am' shows respect; across genders, look toward the speaker's face briefly and keep the gaze lowered.

bodyLanguage.title: Ward-Round Run-Through
bodyLanguage.goal: Combine stance, voice, gaze and gestures in one complete ward-round recommendation.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Prepare a realistic case, e.g. a patient on treatment-dose enoxaparin (1 mg/kg twice daily) whose creatinine clearance has fallen to 25 mL/min.
1:00-2:00 - Enter (b09) and stand grounded at the bedside position (b01) with home-base hands (b06).

2:00-5:00 - Deliver it 3 times on camera: 'Dr. Ahmed, about bed 12. Her creatinine clearance has dropped to 25. I recommend reducing enoxaparin to 1 mg/kg once daily. I'll check an anti-Xa level if needed.' Use a pause before starting, an illustrator gesture on 'reducing', a falling ending, eye contact through the last word, then silence.
5:00-7:00 - Score each take 1-5 for stillness, pace, falling endings, gaze and gestures.
7:00-8:00 - Pick one element to improve on today's real round.
bodyLanguage.why: Skills practised separately need to be combined under realistic conditions before they show up on a real round. Reviewing yourself on video against a simple checklist is a practical form of deliberate practice. Program-design principle, not a specific trial.
bodyLanguage.specter: Bring them the answer, not your homework.

bodyLanguage.title: Negotiation Run-Through
bodyLanguage.goal: Combine anchoring, palm signals, silence and composure in a supplier or formulary negotiation.
steps: 0:00-1:00 - Scenario: agreeing price and terms with a supplier representative for a new formulary product. If procurement in your hospital is centralised and you never negotiate prices, use an internal ask with the same structure instead (e.g. a new clinical pharmacist post or a formulary addition).
1:00-2:00 - Seated (b10): notes laid out, forearms on the table, hands visible.

2:00-5:00 - Deliver to camera: 'We value this partnership. We've reviewed three suppliers. To list this product, the price needs to be 15% lower.' (5 seconds of still silence.) Then answer an imagined pushback: 'I understand. That's our position. If you include training and a 12-month price lock, we can move forward this month.' (Silence.)
5:00-7:00 - Review: open palms on 'we value', palm down on 'needs to be', no self-touch during silences, falling endings.
7:00-8:00 - Deliver the final line once more, cleaner.
bodyLanguage.why: Brings together cues trained separately (b10 seated base, b12 palms, b15 falling endings, b23 silence, b03 stillness). The verbal tactic has the best evidence: in three experiments, whichever side made the first offer tended to get the better outcome, and first offers strongly predicted final prices (Galinsky & Mussweiler, 2001), so anchor on a number you have researched. The body cues range from weak (fidgeting, intonation, silence) to anecdotal (palm direction), so treat them as rehearsing a calm, consistent delivery, not guaranteed tactics.
bodyLanguage.specter: Make your number the one everybody else has to move from.
bodyLanguage.cultural: In Saudi business, start with relationship talk and hospitality (accept the coffee), keep firmness courteous, and never make the other side lose face in front of their colleagues.

bodyLanguage.title: Day-28 Video Audit
bodyLanguage.goal: Measure progress against your Day-1, Day-3 and Day-18 baselines and define your personal presence signature.
steps: 0:00-1:30 - Stand, frame yourself head to feet, and record a 60-second explanation of a recent clinical intervention, the same kind of talk as Day 3 (b03).

1:30-3:00 - Watch on mute: count fidgets (compare with Day 3) and sways or foot shuffles in the first 30 seconds (compare with Day 1). Watch again with sound and count fillers (compare with Day 18). All three baselines used the same length, so compare the numbers directly.
3:00-5:00 - Score each 1-5: grounded stance, posture and chin, stillness, illustrator gestures, palm signals, pace, falling endings, fillers, eye contact through last words, composure.
5:00-6:30 - Your 2 highest scores are your signature strengths. Write one sentence on how you'll use each on rounds this week.
6:30-8:00 - Your 2 lowest scores: schedule those exercises again next week.
bodyLanguage.why: Counting fidgets and fillers shows real change and corrects a documented bias: speakers overestimate how visible their nervousness is to others (the 'illusion of transparency'; Savitsky & Gilovich, 2003). Cycling back to your weakest elements follows deliberate-practice principles. The audit itself is program-design guidance, not a tested protocol.
bodyLanguage.specter: Measure it, fix it, own it.

eyeContact.title: First Contact
eyeContact.goal: Get comfortable meeting a gaze for one short greeting, from first word to last.
steps: Look at the on-screen eyes. Relax your face and drop your shoulders.
Press and hold the button (or the Space bar) as you start the line, keep your eyes on the eyes, and say it at a calm, normal pace.
Release on the last word. The trainer counts a hold of 2 seconds or more, and each line takes about that long. If you finish early, slow down on the next rep instead of holding a silent stare.
Between reps, look away slowly (slightly down) for about 2 seconds, breathe out and blink normally. This is not a staring contest.
Today: greet three same-gender colleagues with your eyes on theirs for the whole greeting, then let your gaze move on naturally.
lines: Good morning, how are you today?
Assalamu alaikum, good morning.
Nice to meet you, I'm the pharmacist.
Thank you, doctor, that's very helpful.
I'll check on that and call you back.
eyeContact.why: A short greeting is the lowest-pressure moment to build the habit of looking at the face while you speak. In Binetti et al. (2016), nearly 500 London Science Museum visitors watched an actor's direct gaze on video. On average they preferred about 3.3 seconds, and most preferred somewhere between 2 and 5 seconds. A 2-second hold sits at the short end of that range, so it's a gentle start. That study measured silent gaze from a face on a screen, not live conversation, so treat the numbers as a rough guide.
eyeContact.cultural: With same-gender peers, direct eye contact during a greeting is expected and reads as sincerity. Across genders, many Saudi Muslims lower their gaze as a religious practice (ghadd al-basar). A brief look at the face, or a lowered gaze with a warm greeting, is fully respectful and still confident. Picture a same-gender colleague for these reps. To practise the opposite-gender or senior version, switch on Respect mode in the trainer, which has you rest your gaze on the face region and lower it at the end.

eyeContact.title: Soft Eyes
eyeContact.goal: Hold gaze with a relaxed, warm face instead of a hard stare.
steps: Before pressing, relax your forehead, jaw and the muscles around your eyes, and let your eyelids rest at their normal height (not widened).
Press and hold as you start the line. Look at the eyes with a slight softening, as you would at a friend, and let a small, genuine smile appear on friendly lines.
Release on the last word. After every 2 reps, check a mirror or your phone camera: are your brows raised or your eyes wide? Relax them.
Today: in one friendly exchange with a same-gender colleague, keep soft eyes for the whole sentence and notice how they respond.
lines: How are you today? It's good to see you.
Thanks for waiting, I'm with you now.
Please take your time, there's no rush at all.
I really appreciate your help with this.
Let's sort this out together, shall we?
It's good to see you back on the ward.
eyeContact.why: Eye contact is read through the face around it. Adams and Kleck (2003) found that direct gaze makes approach emotions such as joy and anger quicker to recognise in a face. This suggests that looking at someone strengthens whatever your expression is already signalling: a relaxed, smiling face reads as friendlier, and a tense brow reads as more hostile. Chen et al. (2013) add that eye contact can come across as a challenge when the listener disagrees. The 'soft eyes' technique itself is coaching, not something that has been tested.
eyeContact.cultural: With same-gender colleagues and patients, a warm smile with eye contact is welcome. Across genders, a smiling, sustained gaze can be misread. Keep the warmth in your voice and words, with a brief look at the face.

eyeContact.title: The Triangle
eyeContact.goal: Move your gaze slowly between the eyes and the bridge of the nose so contact feels natural, not fixed.
steps: Press and hold as you start the line. Begin on one eye and make one slow shift during the line, to the other eye or to the bridge of the nose.
Change the route each rep: left eye to right eye, right eye to nose bridge, nose bridge to left eye. Keep shifts small and slow, never darting.
Release on the last word.
Today: in one conversation where full eye contact feels intense, let your gaze move slowly between the eyes and the nose bridge. Notice that the other person doesn't react.
lines: I've reviewed all of his medications.
The dose looks appropriate for his weight.
Her potassium is normal this morning.
We can switch him to oral this afternoon.
Let me check that interaction for you.
I'll update the chart and let you know.
eyeContact.why: Small shifts within the face aren't seen as breaking eye contact. In the 'eye contact illusion' study (Rogers et al., 2019, Perception; summarised by the BPS Research Digest), a researcher held 4-minute get-to-know-you conversations with 46 people. With half of them he looked mostly at their eyes, and with the other half mostly at their mouth. Both groups reported about the same amount of eye contact and enjoyed the conversation equally: people read gaze anywhere around their face as eye contact. It is one small study, and 'triangle' is a coaching label, not a research term.
eyeContact.cultural: This is especially useful when full eye contact would feel too intense, for example with a senior figure or across genders. It keeps you on the face without fixing on the eyes.

eyeContact.title: Bridge-of-Nose Anchor
eyeContact.goal: Use one anchor point between the eyes when nerves make direct eye contact uncomfortable.
steps: Find the point just above the bridge of the nose, between the on-screen eyes.
Press and hold as you start the line, keep your gaze on that point while you speak, and release on the last word.
Alternate reps between the anchor point and true eye-to-eye contact, and notice which is easier.
Today: use the anchor point in one conversation that makes you nervous. Move toward true eye contact as the week goes on, or keep the anchor as your default where a softer gaze is expected.
lines: Excuse me, doctor, a quick medication question.
The blood culture results are back for bed nine.
I recommend checking a vancomycin level.
Can we review the antibiotics for bed four?
That combination needs closer monitoring.
I'll call you back in ten minutes with the answer.
eyeContact.why: People judge a look as 'at me' across a narrow cone of directions, about 9 degrees wide at 1 metre in Gamer and Hecht's (2007) experiments. In live conversation, people also report the same amount of eye contact whether you look at their eyes or their mouth (Rogers et al., 2019). The bridge of the nose is a few centimetres from the eyes, well inside that cone, so it reads as eye contact while lowering your own anxiety. Both are small lab studies, and the anchor itself is a coaching technique.
eyeContact.cultural: This is a good default for opposite-gender professional conversations and for elders in Saudi settings: it shows attention while staying modest. Lowering the gaze altogether is equally respectful. Respect mode in the trainer practises this face-region gaze.

eyeContact.title: Name, Then Gaze
eyeContact.goal: Lock in eye contact at the moment you say someone's name or title.
steps: Have your eyes on theirs, then press and hold the instant you begin the person's name or title.
Say the name and the sentence while holding gaze. Say the name warmly, with a falling tone.
Release on the last word, pause 1 second, then do the next line.
Today: on rounds, at least three times, look up and meet the person's eyes as you say their name or title (or their face, where a softer gaze fits).
lines: Dr. Khalid, I've reviewed the regimen.
Sister Sara, please hold the 2 p.m. dose.
Abu Fahad, how are you feeling today?
Dr. Noura, the vancomycin level is back.
Mr. Ali, this is your new medication.
Ustadh Saad, thank you for your time today.
eyeContact.why: Pairing a name with eye contact makes it unmistakable who you are addressing and makes the message personal. It is also an easy anchor habit to build. This is a coaching technique; no study has tested this exact pairing.
eyeContact.cultural: Titles such as 'Dr.', 'Ustadh' and the kunya 'Abu Fahad' (father of Fahad) are respectful in Saudi culture. With seniors and elders, pair the title, not just the first name, with your gaze. With opposite-gender colleagues (Sister Sara or Dr. Noura if you are a man, Dr. Khalid or Ustadh Saad if you are a woman), take a brief look at the face as you say the title, then lower your gaze. That keeps it respectful, and Respect mode in the trainer practises it.

eyeContact.title: Hold Through the Last Word
eyeContact.goal: Keep eye contact until the final word of a sentence has landed, instead of looking away early.
steps: Press and hold on the first word, with your eyes on the eyes.
Keep your gaze steady. The urge to look away usually comes in the last 2-3 words, so resist it.
Release once the last word has fully landed (a half-second beat at most). If you looked away early, redo the rep.
Today: on rounds, hold your gaze through the last word of at least two recommendations, then look down at your notes.
lines: I recommend we stop the aspirin today.
This interaction is clinically significant.
This dose is appropriate for her renal function.
We need a vancomycin level before the next dose.
He can go home on this regimen tomorrow.
That's my recommendation, and I'm confident in it.
eyeContact.why: Looking away before you finish can make a solid point look uncertain. In Murphy (2007), looking at your partner while speaking was the behaviour that both tracked measured IQ and raised observers' ratings of intelligence. People trying to seem smart were also able to increase it. A Northeastern University study summarised by the BPS Research Digest likewise found that people who looked at their partner more, especially while talking, were rated as smarter. Separately, Kendon's (1967) recordings of conversations found that speakers usually look at the listener as they finish an utterance, so holding to the end fits natural turn-taking. All of this is correlational or observational, and holding through the last word is an application rather than something tested directly.
eyeContact.cultural: With opposite-gender colleagues or very senior figures, hold on the face region (e03, e08) rather than the eyes, and lower your gaze after the last word. Keep the firmness in your voice.

eyeContact.title: The 3.3-Second Anchor
eyeContact.goal: Calibrate your internal clock to the average gaze length people found comfortable in research.
steps: Press and hold as you start. Say the line at a natural pace, aiming to release at about 3.3 seconds (the trainer's target).
Release on the last word and read the time: were you early or late?
Adjust your pace, not your volume, on the next rep.
Last 2 reps: keep your eyes on the on-screen eyes only, not on the button's timer, and judge about 3 seconds by feel. Check the time after you release.
Today: in one same-gender conversation, notice roughly how long your natural looks last, without trying to change them.
lines: The INR is three point two, just above range.
We can switch to oral levofloxacin today.
I'd suggest reducing the gabapentin dose for his kidneys.
His creatinine clearance is now under thirty.
Let's review this together right after rounds.
I'll prepare the discharge medications now.
eyeContact.why: In Binetti et al. (2016, Royal Society Open Science), nearly 500 London Science Museum visitors from 56 nations watched clips of an actor making eye contact for between 0.1 and 10.3 seconds. After each clip they said whether it felt too short or too long. The average preferred duration was about 3.3 seconds, most people preferred between about 2 and 5 seconds, and nobody preferred less than 1 second or more than 9. Preference did not depend on the viewer's gender, personality or how attractive they found the actor. The limits: this was silent gaze from an actor on video, not a live conversation (where looks are broken up by speech and glances away), and people differed. Treat 3.3 seconds as a calibration point, not a rule.
eyeContact.cultural: The 3.3-second figure comes from a multinational museum sample in London. In Saudi settings it fits same-gender peers of similar age and status. Use a shorter, softer or lowered gaze across genders or with very senior figures and elders (Respect mode).

eyeContact.title: Respect Mode: Seniors and Opposite Gender
eyeContact.goal: Practise a shorter, softer, respectful gaze for senior figures or opposite-gender colleagues while still sounding fully confident.
steps: Switch on Respect mode in the trainer. It caps the target at 3 seconds and counts holds between 3 and 4 seconds.
Press and hold as you start. Rest your gaze on the face region (triangle or bridge of the nose) rather than locking onto the eyes, and say the line calmly.

On the last word, release and lower your gaze slowly and slightly downward (not sideways), with a small nod. If a line runs past 3 seconds, lower your gaze and release there, then finish the sentence with your eyes lowered.
Keep your voice and posture fully confident; only the gaze softens.
Today: use this with one senior figure or opposite-gender colleague, and notice that the firmness carries through your words and tone.
lines: Dr. Abdullah, may I raise one quick concern, please?
With respect, doctor, I'd suggest a lower dose.
Thank you, Dr. Huda. I'll follow up this afternoon.
The committee has approved the new protocol.
I'll send you the written summary this evening.
eyeContact.why: Confidence doesn't require a dominant stare. Cultural Atlas notes that in Saudi Arabia direct eye contact is expected between people of the same age, gender or status. It also notes that men and women commonly lower their gaze with each other, and that younger people may lower their gaze with elders out of respect. For many Muslims, lowering the gaze between unrelated men and women is a religious instruction (Qur'an 24:30-31). In 'visual dominance' research (Dovidio & Ellyson, 1982), people who look at others as much while speaking as while listening were judged more powerful. That suggests a long, level gaze at a senior can read as a status claim. The hold here is deliberately shorter than e07.
eyeContact.cultural: Many Saudi colleagues, men and women, practise lowering the gaze between unrelated men and women (ghadd al-basar): look at the face briefly to show attention, then lower your gaze. This is a mark of good manners and faith, not a lack of confidence. With elders and very senior consultants, a softer gaze likewise signals respect.

eyeContact.title: Numbers With Your Eyes
eyeContact.goal: Say key clinical numbers while holding gaze, instead of reading them off the chart.
steps: Read the line once, then look up at the eyes.
Press and hold and say the whole line from memory, with eye contact.
Release after the unit or final word.
Real-life rule: if you need your notes, look down, read, look up, then speak the number.
Today: present at least one lab value or dose on rounds this way.
lines: The vancomycin level came back high, so we hold the next dose.
Her creatinine clearance is 25 mL per minute.
Potassium is 5.9, so I recommend holding the spironolactone.
The INR is 4.1, with no signs of bleeding.
For vancomycin, we're targeting an AUC of 400 to 600.
Give enoxaparin 40 mg once daily for prophylaxis.
eyeContact.why: Reading the key number off a page while you say it breaks contact at the most important moment. 'Look down, read, look up, speak' separates reading from speaking, so your gaze is on the person when the number and the conclusion land. This is public-speaking practice, not a tested finding.
eyeContact.cultural: On rounds with a senior consultant or an opposite-gender colleague, keep the same look-down, read, look-up rhythm, but deliver the number to the face region with a shorter look. The clarity of the number matters more than the length of the gaze. In Respect mode the trainer caps the target at 3 seconds: look at the face, release at about 3 seconds as you lower your gaze, and finish the sentence with your eyes lowered.

eyeContact.title: Break Down, Not Sideways
eyeContact.goal: End eye contact calmly with a slow downward glance (to notes or chart) rather than a quick sideways dart.
steps: Press and hold as you start, say the line with eye contact, and release on the last word.
Then do the break. Type A is a slow glance down to an imagined chart for about 1 second, then back up. On one rep only, do Type B, a quick sideways dart, to feel the contrast.
All other reps: Type A only.
Optional: watch yourself in a mirror or on camera and judge which looks composed.
Today: whenever you need to break eye contact on rounds, break downward to your notes or the chart, slowly.
lines: Let me check the chart before I confirm that dose for you.
I'll confirm the dose and come back to you in five minutes.
The allergy is documented as a mild rash, not anaphylaxis.
We can give this one through the NG tube; it's safe to crush.
There's an alternative on our formulary that works just as well.
I'll write up the plan now and update the whole team.
eyeContact.why: Breaking gaze is normal and necessary. Glenberg et al. (1998) found that people look away more as questions get harder, and that looking away improves their answers. How you break also affects impressions: a slow, purposeful glance at your notes looks like thinking, while rapid sideways darting is commonly read as evasive. That second part is coaching wisdom, not a tested finding.
eyeContact.cultural: A downward break is also the respectful way to end gaze with elders and across genders in Saudi Arabia.

eyeContact.title: Look Away to Think, Return to Deliver
eyeContact.goal: Look away while you think, then come back to eye contact for the answer.
steps: Read the bracketed question silently, as if it had just been asked.
With the button released, look slightly down or away for 1-2 seconds while you think.
Look back at the eyes, press and hold, and deliver the answer (the unbracketed part).
Release on the last word.
Today: when someone asks you a hard question, give yourself 1-2 seconds looking down to think, then look up for the answer.
lines: [Can we crush this tablet?] No, it's extended-release; I'll suggest an alternative.
[Is it safe in pregnancy?] Yes, labetalol is a preferred first-line option in pregnancy.
[Why the dose change?] Her kidney function has dropped this week, so the drug would build up.
[Do we need a level?] Yes, two vancomycin levels, so we can estimate the AUC.
[Can she take the calcium with the ciprofloxacin?] Yes, if the ciprofloxacin goes two hours before or six hours after it.
[Is it on formulary?] Not this one, but there's an equivalent we can use today.
eyeContact.why: Glenberg et al. (1998) found that people look away more as questions get harder, and that looking away improves recall, apparently because it cuts out visual input that competes with thinking. Follow-up studies in children and older adults found similar benefits. So don't force eye contact while you think; bring it back for the conclusion, where it signals certainty.
eyeContact.cultural: With a senior consultant, a brief downward look while you think reads as careful and respectful. It is also the natural pattern across genders.

eyeContact.title: Listening Gaze
eyeContact.goal: Keep a steady, relaxed gaze while listening, with short acknowledgments.
steps: Imagine the person on screen is describing a problem to you.
Press and hold, then 'listen' silently for about 2 seconds with one slow nod, a soft attentive face and normal blinking.
Then say the acknowledgment line, still holding gaze, and release on the last word.
No fidgeting between reps.
Today: in one conversation, keep a relaxed gaze on the speaker's face while they talk, glancing away now and then, and acknowledge with a nod or a short line.
lines: I see, that makes sense.
Go on, I'm listening.
So the main concern is the bleeding risk.
Understood, thank you for flagging it.
Tell me more about that.
When did you first notice it?
eyeContact.why: Listeners normally look at a speaker more than speakers look at listeners, so steady gaze while listening is expected rather than intense. In the Northeastern University study summarised by the BPS Research Digest, people who looked at their partner more were rated as smarter. The effect was mainly while they were talking and weaker while listening, so the listening link is the weaker one. Visual-dominance research (Dovidio & Ellyson, 1982) adds a nuance: looking much more while listening than while speaking is read as lower power. Pair this drill with e06 rather than relying on it alone. Above all, steady, relaxed listening gaze tells the speaker you're with them.
eyeContact.cultural: When listening to an elder or a senior, a softer gaze with frequent nods and a quiet 'na'am' is respectful. Across genders, attentive nods and a lowered gaze show you are listening just as well.

eyeContact.title: Answering a Challenge
eyeContact.goal: Hold steady eye contact while responding calmly to a challenge, then move the focus to the evidence.
steps: Read the bracketed challenge silently and pause 1 second.
Press and hold, meet the eyes (or the face region), and deliver the response at a calm pace.
Hold through the last word, then release and glance down at an imagined chart, as if bringing them to the evidence.
Keep a neutral or slightly warm face: no apologetic smile, no frown.
Today: the next time you're challenged, keep your eyes up through your answer, then turn both your attention and theirs to the chart or guideline.
lines: [Why are you questioning my order?] Because the dose exceeds the renal maximum; here's an alternative.
[We always use this antibiotic.] I understand, but the culture shows resistance, so it won't work here.
[Just approve it.] I can't approve it as written, but I can approve this modification.
[That's not your area.] Medication safety is my responsibility; let's decide this together.
[Are you sure?] Yes, I'm sure. I checked the guideline and both of the levels.
[It's urgent.] Then let's correct the dose now, and I'll make sure it goes up immediately.
eyeContact.why: Dropping your eyes and speeding up while you answer a challenge looks like retreat; steady gaze while you calmly give your reasoning looks composed. But the person here already disagrees with you. Chen et al. (2013) found that listeners who disagree are persuaded less when they look a speaker in the eyes, possibly because eye contact reads as a challenge in that situation. Adams and Kleck (2003) also found that direct gaze makes anger quicker to read in a face. So keep the hold to your sentence, keep your face calm, and then shift attention to shared evidence. This combination is coaching, not a tested protocol.
eyeContact.cultural: If the challenger is a senior consultant, handle it privately where possible, use 'Dr.' and a respectful tone, and use the Respect-mode gaze from e08. In Respect mode the trainer caps the target at 3 seconds: look at the face, release at about 3 seconds as you lower your gaze, and finish the sentence with your eyes lowered.

eyeContact.title: Saying No With Your Eyes
eyeContact.goal: Deliver a refusal or limit while holding gaze, without softening it with a nervous smile or looking away.
steps: Press and hold as you start, with your eyes on the eyes.
Say the line in a calm, falling tone while keeping eye contact.
Hold about 1 second of silence after the last word, then release. The line plus that beat reaches the 4-second target. Don't stretch the silence to get there; slow your delivery instead.
No nervous laugh and no repeated 'sorry, sorry'. One polite opener is fine.
Today: deliver one 'no' or limit with your eyes up through the last word, then stop talking.
lines: With respect, I can't dispense that without a prescription.
I'm sorry, but that's not something we can do.
I won't approve a dose above the maximum.
No, we need to wait for the level before we give it.
I'm afraid that price doesn't work for our budget this year.
I'm not able to make an exception this time.
eyeContact.why: A refusal said while looking away or smiling apologetically is easily heard as negotiable, while steady gaze plus a short silence signals that the limit is real. This is coaching practice, not a specific study. Keep your face neutral rather than hard: with someone who already disagrees, prolonged eye contact can increase resistance (Chen et al., 2013).
eyeContact.cultural: Saudi communication often softens refusals to save face. A respectful opener ('With respect...', 'I'm sorry, but...') keeps it polite while your gaze keeps it firm. Across genders or with seniors, a brief look and a lowered gaze is enough; the firmness lives in your words and tone.

eyeContact.title: One Thought, One Person
eyeContact.goal: Meeting rule: deliver one complete thought to one person, then move to the next.
steps: Imagine three people at the table: left, centre and right. The on-screen eyes are whoever you're addressing now.
Press and hold for the whole sentence to one person, then release on the last word.
Turn your head slightly as if to the next person, then press and hold again for the next sentence.
Never move your eyes mid-sentence; switch only between thoughts.
Today: in your next meeting or MDT, deliver at least three sentences this way, one person per sentence.
lines: We have a problem with his current vancomycin regimen.
His kidney function has dropped, so the dose is now too high.
I recommend extending the interval to every 48 hours.
I'll adjust the order with the team before the next dose is due.
Nursing, please hold the next dose until the level comes back.
We'll recheck his creatinine and a level on Thursday morning.
eyeContact.why: Scanning a group continuously (the 'lighthouse') leaves no one feeling addressed; finishing a thought with one person creates a series of real one-to-one connections. This is widely taught in public speaking but not directly tested. It fits the finding that looking at your listener while speaking is linked to perceived intelligence (Murphy, 2007).
eyeContact.cultural: Include everyone, opposite-gender colleagues too, but give them a shorter, face-region or lowered look where a full hold would be inappropriate.

eyeContact.title: Anchor the Number
eyeContact.goal: State your number or request in a negotiation while holding gaze, without hedging.
steps: Press and hold as you start.
Say the number or request clearly, with a falling tone.
Keep holding, in calm silence, for 1-2 seconds after the last word, then release. If you're short of the target, slow your delivery next time rather than stretching the silence.
Keep a calm, neutral face: steady, not challenging.
Today: state one number or request (a dose, a deadline, a staffing ask) with your eyes up and a short silence after it.
lines: Our budget for this contract is 1.2 million riyals.
We need the price to be fifteen percent lower.
Delivery within 48 hours is a requirement.
We'd need a twelve-month price lock on all three products.
I need two protected hours a day for clinical rounds.
That's our offer, and we think it's a fair one.
eyeContact.why: The moment you state a number is when a wavering gaze or rising tone does the most damage, because it signals that the number is flexible. This is negotiation-training practice. Eye contact can increase resistance in an already sceptical listener (Chen et al., 2013), so keep a calm, neutral face rather than a challenging stare.
eyeContact.cultural: Saudi negotiations are relationship-driven. State numbers firmly, but after rapport, and keep it courteous. With a senior director, a steady look at the face region while you state the request is enough.

eyeContact.title: Hold Through the Silence
eyeContact.goal: Keep a relaxed gaze and stillness during a short silence after your point.
steps: Press and hold as you start the line.
Say the line (about 2 seconds).
Keep holding in silence until the target, about 2 more seconds, with a relaxed face, normal blinking and steady breath.
Release with a small nod.

Today: after your next recommendation or question, stay quiet and keep a relaxed gaze for 2-3 seconds instead of filling the silence. If the silence goes on, soften your gaze or glance at your notes rather than keep looking.
lines: Those are the terms we can offer.
That's what the evidence supports here.
I'd rather we stop it now than wait.
The final decision is yours, doctor.
What would make this work for you?
Take your time; I'll wait for your answer.
eyeContact.why: Silence after a point lets it land and invites a response; looking away at once or filling the gap often reads as discomfort. The total gaze here, about 4.5 seconds, is near the top of the 2-5 second range most people preferred in Binetti et al. (2016), so it is at the edge of comfortable. Silent gaze much longer than this starts to read as staring. This is coaching practice.
eyeContact.cultural: Keep your expression warm during the silence; a cold stare can feel disrespectful in Saudi settings. Across genders or with seniors, hold the stillness but lower your gaze during the silence rather than keep eye contact.

eyeContact.title: Pushback Without Flinching
eyeContact.goal: Keep a relaxed, steady gaze while someone disagrees with you, then restate your position calmly.
steps: Press and hold as the imagined pushback begins. Read the bracketed words silently, as if hearing them, while keeping a relaxed, steady gaze: that's you listening.
Then say your response calmly and release on the last word.
Watch for bursts of blinking, dropping your eyes, or a flinch-smile while the pushback 'lands'.
After releasing, glance down at an imagined chart, as if inviting them to look at the evidence with you.
Today: when someone pushes back, keep your eyes on them while they speak, acknowledge first, give a one-sentence answer, then look at the data together rather than holding the stare.
lines: [That's too expensive.] I understand. One serious error would cost far more.
[The patient wants the brand.] I understand. The generic is bioequivalent.
[Your recommendation is overkill.] I hear you. The interaction risk justifies it.
[Other hospitals don't do this.] Perhaps, but our policy follows the guideline.
[We don't have time.] It takes two minutes and prevents a serious error.
[I disagree.] That's fair. Let's look at the culture results together.
eyeContact.why: Holding a steady gaze while the other person disagrees, then acknowledging their view and calmly restating yours, shows composure under pressure. Unlike e13, the hold here covers listening as well as answering. Your gaze should say 'steady', not 'challenge': Chen et al. (2013) found that eye contact can increase resistance in someone who already disagrees. That is why the response is short and is followed by a shift to shared evidence. This is a coaching application of a lab finding.
eyeContact.cultural: With seniors or across genders, use the Respect-mode gaze (e08): calm, courteous words with a softer or lowered gaze rather than locked eyes.

eyeContact.title: Warm Gaze vs Firm Gaze
eyeContact.goal: Switch on purpose between warm gaze (rapport) and firm gaze (decision).
steps: Odd reps (1, 3, 5) are WARM: soft eyes, slight smile, relaxed head.
Even reps (2, 4, 6) are FIRM: neutral face, level head, still body.
Press and hold as you start, deliver the line in the matching mode, and release on the last word.
Check a mirror or camera now and then: does your face match the words?
Today: use a warm gaze in one greeting and a firm gaze in one decision, and notice how people respond to each.
lines: It's really good to be working with you again, Dr. Sami.
We pause the vancomycin now and restart it at a slower rate.
How is the family? I hope everyone is doing well these days.
This needs to change today, before the next dose is given.
Thank you, I really appreciate you staying late for this.
My answer is no, and I'm not going to change it today.
eyeContact.why: The same eye contact means different things depending on the face around it. Adams and Kleck (2003) found that direct gaze makes joy and anger quicker to read in a face, consistent with gaze amplifying what your expression already says. Chen et al. (2013) suggested that eye contact signals connection to people who agree with you but challenge to people who don't, so choosing the mode deliberately matters.
eyeContact.cultural: Picture same-gender colleagues for these reps. Across genders, warmth and firmness come from your tone and words with a brief glance, not a long hold. Asking a man about his family is usually phrased generally ('How is the family?'), not about his wife by name.

eyeContact.title: Group Rhythm: Three People
eyeContact.goal: Apply one-thought-one-person to a three-person group with longer sentences.
steps: Assign Dr. A (left), Dr. B (centre) and Nurse C (right).
For each rep, turn your head slightly to that person, press and hold as you start, deliver the thought, and release on the last word.
Cover all three by rep 3, then go round again.
Include the quietest person, not only the most senior.
Today: on rounds or in a huddle, give each person at least one full sentence of your attention.
lines: Dr. A, cefepime is the right choice, but this dose is too low for him.
Dr. B, I'd suggest two grams every eight hours while his kidneys are normal.
Nurse C, please give each dose as an extended infusion over three hours.
Dr. A, I'll check his creatinine daily and adjust the dose if it rises.
Dr. B, I'll update the order as soon as we finish rounds this morning.
Nurse C, please call me if he becomes confused or develops a rash.
