eyeContact.why: This extends e15 to longer, multi-person delivery, which is the real format of ward rounds and MDT meetings. It is coaching practice.
eyeContact.cultural: Address the most senior person first, then include everyone. Give opposite-gender colleagues a shorter, face-region or lowered look.

eyeContact.title: Owning the Close
eyeContact.goal: Hold gaze on the closing line of a recommendation or negotiation and finish cleanly.
steps: Press and hold as you start. Say the closing line slowly, with a falling tone.
Hold through the last word plus a silent beat of about 1 second.
Then give a slow nod, release, and make a slow downward glance to your notes.
No 'if that's okay?' tag at the end.
Today: close one recommendation or meeting this way: a summary sentence, a beat and a nod.
lines: Then we're agreed. I'll update the order right after rounds.
So we switch to oral today and review him tomorrow morning.
If the final terms are confirmed in writing, we can sign this week.
I'll send the final terms to your office this afternoon.
Good. We'll proceed with the lower dose and recheck on Sunday.
Thank you, everyone. I'll take it from here and update you tomorrow.
eyeContact.why: The close is where uncertainty shows most: trailing off, looking down early, or adding 'if that's okay?'. Holding gaze through a short summary and then nodding marks the decision as made. This is coaching practice.
eyeContact.cultural: Across genders or with very senior figures, close with a brief look, a slow nod and a lowered gaze rather than a long hold.

eyeContact.title: Social Storytelling Gaze
eyeContact.goal: Use warm eye contact in social conversation (majlis, dinner, a conference coffee break), coming back to the person at the key moments.
steps: Imagine telling a short story to one person over coffee.
Press and hold as you start, with a warm face, and deliver the line with expression. Release on the last word.
Between lines, glance away naturally, then come back. In real storytelling you'll often look away as you start a sentence and come back for its end.
Let natural smiles happen; this is social, not a negotiation.
Today: in one social chat, look back at the person at the end of each key sentence and whenever you ask them a question.
lines: You won't believe what happened on the ward this morning.
I went into pharmacy because of my grandfather's medicines.
The best advice I ever got was to ask one more question.
The funniest thing happened at the conference last week.
Tell me, how did you get into this field in the first place?
That's a great story! So what did you do after that?
eyeContact.why: Social charisma combines presence with warmth: friendly eye contact and genuine interest. Kendon's (1967) recordings of conversation found that speakers usually look away as they begin a longer utterance and look back at the listener as they finish it, though later studies only partly confirmed this. So a story naturally alternates glances away with returns at the key moments, and the hold here is shorter than in the professional drills for that reason. The Northeastern University study summarised by the BPS Research Digest, linking eye contact while talking to perceived intelligence, used casual conversations between strangers, so it applies socially too. The rest is coaching guidance.
eyeContact.cultural: In a majlis or family gathering, warm eye contact with same-gender peers is natural. With elders, a softer gaze and attentive listening are valued as much as good storytelling. With opposite-gender guests or colleagues, keep glances brief and let warmth come through your words and attention.

eyeContact.title: The Long Recommendation
eyeContact.goal: Hold eye contact across a two-part recommendation: the finding, then the action.
steps: Press and hold as you start, and deliver both sentences as one connected thought, with a falling tone at the end.
On the trainer, releasing ends the rep, so keep the button held through both sentences. If you lose your place, finish the line anyway and redo the rep.
Hold through the very last word, then release slowly with a nod.
Real life: a brief glance at your notes between the two sentences is normal. Bring your eyes back for the action sentence.
Today: deliver one two-part recommendation (finding, then action) with your eyes on the person for the action.
lines: Her creatinine clearance is 25. I'd reduce levetiracetam to 500 twice daily.
The culture grew MRSA. I recommend vancomycin with AUC-guided dosing.
He's had two falls in the last month. I suggest we taper the zolpidem down and then stop it.
The INR is 4.5 with no bleeding. I'd hold one warfarin dose and recheck tomorrow.
Meropenem will drop his valproate level. I recommend a different antibiotic.
eyeContact.why: Real recommendations often run longer than one breath. A 6-second hold is longer than most people's preferred length for silent mutual gaze (most preferred 2-5 seconds in Binetti et al., 2016). This is deliberate overload. It is filled with speech, which feels very different from a silent stare, and it is meant to make 3-4 second holds on rounds feel easy. That training logic has not been tested, and in real conversation speakers usually glance away between sentences (Kendon, 1967). Don't carry unbroken 6-second holds into real life.
eyeContact.cultural: With seniors or across genders, split this into two shorter face-region looks, or a brief look and a lowered gaze, rather than one long hold. In Respect mode the trainer caps the target at 3 seconds: look at the face, release at about 3 seconds as you lower your gaze, and finish the sentence with your eyes lowered.

eyeContact.title: Recover a Lost Gaze
eyeContact.goal: If you break eye contact mid-sentence, return calmly and finish strong.
steps: Press and hold as you start the line.
At the bracket, glance down for about 1 second while still holding the button. The trainer times the whole line, glance included.
Come back to the eyes calmly, with no apology and no restart, and finish with a falling tone.
Release after the last word.
Today: if you lose eye contact mid-sentence, just come back and finish. Notice that nobody reacts.
lines: The vancomycin level is [glance down] within range, so no change today.
I recommend [glance down] switching from warfarin to apixaban.
We'll need [glance down] a repeat potassium at six this evening.
Our offer is [glance down] final for this quarter, and it includes training.
The interaction [glance down] is moderate, so we'll monitor her INR.
Let's proceed [glance down] with the plan we agreed this morning.
eyeContact.why: Losing eye contact is normal. What reads as nerves is the scramble afterwards: apologising, restarting, rushing. Returning calmly and finishing shows composure. This is coaching practice.
eyeContact.cultural: The same rule applies with seniors and across genders: a calm return to the face region (or a lowered gaze), with no apology.

eyeContact.title: Pressure Hold
eyeContact.goal: State a firm position and stay still and composed through a silence under imagined pressure.
steps: Imagine a tense negotiation or a frustrated consultant across from you.
Press and hold as you start, and state the position (about 3-4 seconds).
Keep holding in silence, with a relaxed face and steady breath, until the target (about 2-3 seconds of silence).
Release with a slow nod and a slow downward glance.
Real life: this silent hold is longer than is comfortable, on purpose. With a real person, after about 2 seconds of silence, soften your gaze or look at your notes while staying physically still.
lines: Patient safety comes first, so I can't approve this dose.
Our final offer is 1.1 million riyals, and it won't change.
I won't sign off on this until the level is back.
This change needs the committee's approval before we start.
That's our position, and I'm comfortable with it.
eyeContact.why: This is training overload. The total gaze (about 6 seconds, including the silence) is beyond the 2-5 seconds most people preferred in Binetti et al. (2016), and holding it under imagined stress is meant to build tolerance so that normal holds feel easy. That idea is untested. In real life, a long stare at someone who already disagrees can increase their resistance (Chen et al., 2013) and would read as staring. Use this as practice, then apply shorter, calmer holds.
eyeContact.cultural: In real Saudi workplace conflict, especially with seniors, a long fixed stare would be seen as confrontational. Put the firmness in your words and voice, and soften or lower your gaze.

eyeContact.title: The Executive Introduction
eyeContact.goal: Introduce yourself to a director, committee or new consultant with steady, confident gaze.
steps: Press and hold as you start, and deliver each line as part of one introduction.
Hold through the last word, with a falling tone, then release.
Between reps, make a brief downward glance, then come back.
Fill in the brackets with your real details and say them the same way each time.
This week: introduce yourself this way to one new consultant, director or committee member.
lines: Assalamu alaikum. I'm the clinical pharmacist for the medical wards.
I've been a clinical pharmacist in this hospital for [X] years.
My focus this year is reducing medication errors at discharge.
I'd value ten minutes with you next week to share our data.
It's a pleasure to meet you, and I look forward to working with you.
eyeContact.why: A short, confident self-introduction with steady eye contact is a high-impact moment in a hospital (new consultants, directors, committees), and it's predictable, so you can rehearse it. The hold is moderate because the audience is usually senior: in Saudi settings a long, level gaze at a director can read as presumptuous (see e08). This is coaching practice.
eyeContact.cultural: Greet the most senior person first, and use 'Assalamu alaikum' and titles. With opposite-gender leaders, use the Respect-mode gaze and don't initiate a handshake. If one is offered and you don't shake hands across genders, a hand on the heart with a warm greeting is polite.

eyeContact.title: Real-Life Transfer Day
eyeContact.goal: Warm up on the trainer, then complete three real eye-contact missions today.
steps: Trainer warm-up: 5 reps at the 4-second target with the lines below. Press as you start and release on the last word.
Mission 1 (ward round): hold your gaze through the last word of one recommendation.
Mission 2 (meeting): use one-thought-one-person for at least 3 sentences.
Mission 3 (social): one warm look of roughly 3 seconds, with a genuine smile, when greeting a same-gender colleague you know.
Tonight: note which mission felt hardest and run that drill once more (e06, e15 or e22) before tomorrow's final.
lines: I recommend we stop the PPI, since there's no ongoing indication.
I suggest we start with the highest-risk patients on today's list.
Our latest audit shows fewer errors since we changed the process.
We can implement this on all the medical wards next month.
Thank you all; I'll circulate the plan by the end of today.
eyeContact.why: Skills practised on a screen don't automatically carry over to real conversations, and specific real-world missions bridge that gap. This is a general practice-design principle, not something tested for eye-contact training. The warm-up target returns to 4 seconds, about one spoken sentence, which fits real conversation.
eyeContact.cultural: Pick missions that suit the person: full holds with same-gender peers, and the Respect-mode gaze with seniors and opposite-gender colleagues.

eyeContact.title: Final Exam: Full Case Under Pressure
eyeContact.goal: Deliver a complete case recommendation with full-sentence holds, controlled breaks and a clean close.
steps: Treat the 8 reps as one continuous case presentation. Press and hold as you start each line, and release on its last word.
Between reps, glance down to 'your notes' and come back.
Hold through every last word, with a falling tone.
On the last rep, ask the question, hold a short silent beat, give a slow nod and release.
Then present the same case to your phone camera and compare it with your Day 3 recording (b03). Where do your eyes go when you give numbers and recommendations?
lines: Good morning, Dr. Faisal. I'd like to discuss the patient in bed 12 with you.
She's 78, with atrial fibrillation and declining kidney function.
Over three months, her creatinine clearance has fallen to 28.
She's still on rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, which is now too high.
I recommend reducing it to 15 mg once daily with her evening meal.
We should also stop the ibuprofen; it adds bleeding risk and strains her kidneys.
I'll recheck her kidney function next week and adjust again if it changes.
So that's 15 mg with her evening meal and no ibuprofen. Do you agree?
eyeContact.why: This brings everything together: name plus gaze, numbers with your eyes, holding through the last word, controlled breaks and the close. The target settles at 5 seconds, about one full spoken sentence, which is the skill you'll use on real rounds; the 6-second overload days were preparation. This is a practice-design principle, not a tested protocol.
eyeContact.cultural: If the consultant is very senior or of the opposite gender, use the Respect-mode gaze while keeping the same confident words and voice. In Respect mode the trainer caps the target at 3 seconds: look at the face, release at about 3 seconds as you lower your gaze, and finish the sentence with your eyes lowered.
